hook: **You can't improve what you don't measure.** In GenAI, the model's mood is not a metric. Evals are how quality becomes engineering instead of vibes.

scenes.title: Prompts drift. Models drift. **Only evals notice.**
scenes.narration: Every change in a GenAI system — new prompt wording, a new model version, a new chunk size — is a bet on quality. Without evals, you find out whether the bet paid off from user complaints. Three forces make change constant: prompt iteration never ends; models update silently — a provider's 'gpt-same-name' behaves differently in March than January; and your DATA changes — new documents, edited policies. Evals convert all three from surprises into detected, measurable deltas. The rule that changes culture: no prompt change, model swap, or pipeline tweak ships without an eval run — the same discipline as unit tests for code, applied to behavior.

items.s: 'small wording fix' is a quality bet — evals settle whether it paid
Same model name, new behavior · evals detect drift you can't see by vibe
Re-indexed corpora change answers · evals catch freshness regressions

scenes.narration: A concrete story for each force. Prompt iteration: 'just make it friendlier' subtly drops citation rigor — an eval measuring citation coverage catches it in the PR, not in a customer call. Silent updates: providers fine-tune and re-deploy under the same model name; your golden set run weekly becomes a drift alarm. Living data: the corpus you re-indexed Tuesday now answers 'refund window' from a deprecated policy page; the eval flags the regression before users do. The unifying point: in classical software, code that passes tests behaves the same tomorrow. In GenAI, passing behavior decays on its own — evals are the only regression defense.

scenes.title: The golden dataset: **fifty questions you trust completely**
scenes.sub: Small, curated, versioned — the anchor of everything
scenes.narration: The golden dataset is your source of truth: fifty to a few hundred real questions, each with a known-correct answer or grading criteria, drawn from actual user queries and reviewed by domain experts. Quality beats size — two hundred vetted questions outperform ten thousand noisy ones. Cover the shape of reality: common questions, edge cases, adversarial inputs, and — critically — UNANSWERABLE questions, so abstention is measured, not assumed. Version it like code: golden-v1, golden-v2 — when you add cases, the dataset grows deliberately, and old versions stay runnable so you can compare runs across time. This dataset is also GA-15's recall-measuring tool and GA-16's abstention test — one artifact, many evals.

items.s: From actual logs + SME review · a wrong 'golden' answer corrupts every metric downstream
Common · edge · adversarial · unanswerable → measures hits AND honesty
golden-v1, v2… · every eval run records WHICH dataset version scored it

scenes.narration: Build it incrementally: start with fifty questions from support tickets and sales calls — the questions users actually ask, not the ones you imagine. Get subject-matter experts to write reference answers and, importantly, grading guidance: some answers are exact-match, others need rubric judgments — 'must mention X, must not claim Y'. Then treat contamination as the enemy: golden questions must never leak into few-shot prompts or fine-tuning data, or your eval measures memorization. Finally, budget maintenance: assign an owner; a stale golden set measuring last year's product is worse than none — schedule quarterly reviews against current docs and fresh logs. The dataset is infrastructure, with all that implies.

scenes.title: Two eval arenas: **the lab and the field**
scenes.sub: Offline before release, online after — each catches different failures
scenes.narration: Offline evals run pre-release: the golden dataset, fixed inputs, reproducible scores — your regression gate, comparable run-over-run. Their blind spot: the golden set is a SAMPLE of reality, and reality is wider. Online evals run in production: sampled real traffic scored in shadow — the system answers the user AND a judge scores the exchange. Three online patterns: shadow judging — score a copy of production traffic without affecting users; user feedback — thumbs, ratings, reported issues, cheap and biased but directional; canary analysis — route five percent of traffic to the new prompt and compare quality metrics against the control. The rule: offline gates every release; online monitors every hour.

cards.s: Reproducible · comparable · gates releases · limited by sample coverage
Real distribution, real drift detection · noisier · needs sampling + privacy care

scenes.narration: How they compose into a pipeline: every PR runs offline evals — fast subset, fifty cases, minutes; nightly runs the full golden set; release requires no-regression. In production, sample one to five percent of traffic for shadow judging — enough signal, manageable cost. Wire alerts on deltas, not absolutes: 'faithfulness dropped twelve percent week-over-week' pages someone; a single bad score doesn't. One more distinction that saves confusion: offline evals measure the SYSTEM's changeability — did my edit help? Online evals measure reality's drift — is the world different? You need both questions answered continuously, and conflating them is how teams ship confidently into a silently degraded product.

scenes.title: When the judge is a person: **calibrate first**
scenes.sub: SME review loops that scale without rotting
scenes.narration: Some quality dimensions resist automation: brand voice, legal nuance, clinical correctness — domains where an LLM judge hallucinating a grade is worse than no grade. Human review is the ground truth for those — but raw human judgment drifts between reviewers and within one reviewer across a long session. The fix is calibration: run the same twenty cases past every reviewer, compare judgments, discuss disagreements until the rubric is understood identically — THEN start production review. Inter-rater agreement — measured, say, with Cohen's kappa — becomes a health metric for the review process itself. And close the loop: human verdicts feed back into better golden sets and better LLM-judge prompts — people calibrate the machines that will absorb most of the volume.

layers.s: Shared 20-case set · discussion · Cohen's kappa ≥ target before production review
Random + flagged cases · rubric-driven, not vibes
Verdicts → golden set additions + judge-prompt improvements

scenes.narration: The scaled review loop. Sampling strategy matters: purely random sampling misses the tail — mix in FLAGGED cases: low retrieval scores, user thumbs-down, abstentions, unusually long answers. Reviewers with a rubric grade consistently; reviewers without one grade their mood. Budget honestly: full human review doesn't scale to millions of requests, and isn't needed — review to CALIBRATE the automated layer, then let automation carry the volume with humans auditing a shrinking percentage. The failure mode to avoid is review theater: high review volume, no disagreement discussions, kappa unmeasured — that's cost without quality. Measure the reviewers the way you measure the models, or neither number means anything.

scenes.title: Eval culture established. Now the specific metrics.
scenes.next: Reel 40 · RAG & LLM Metrics — faithfulness, context recall, LLM-as-judge

recap: Change is constant (prompts, silent model updates, living data) — evals are the only regression defense in GenAI
Golden dataset: 50–200 expert-reviewed real questions, versioned like code, including unanswerable cases; quality over size
Offline gates releases, online monitors drift; human review calibrates machines — measure the reviewers too

quiz.q: Why is a wrong 'golden' answer especially damaging?
opts: Every metric computed against it is corrupted — you're optimizing toward a wrong target
quiz.why: The golden set is the anchor of all measurement; SME review exists precisely because one bad reference answer skews every downstream score.

quiz.q: What must a golden dataset include to measure abstention?
opts: Unanswerable questions — otherwise 'never says no' scores the same as 'honest'
quiz.why: Without unanswerable cases, abstention is untestable — the system gets no credit for honesty and no penalty for confabulation.

quiz.q: What is Cohen's kappa measuring in a human review loop?
opts: Inter-rater agreement beyond chance — the health metric of the review process itself
quiz.why: Low kappa means reviewers disagree systematically — grading noise, not product signal; calibrate before trusting verdicts.

code.title: Versioned golden set + offline eval runner
code.body:
# golden/v2.jsonl  — versioned like code, reviewed by SMEs
{"q": "What is the refund window?", "must_contain": ["30 days"], "answerable": true}
{"q": "Who is the CEO's dentist?",    "answerable": false}   # abstain expected

# eval_runner.py
import json, datetime

def run_golden(pipeline, version: str) -> dict:
    cases = [json.loads(l) for l in open(f"golden/{version}.jsonl")]
    rows = []
    for c in cases:
        out = pipeline.ask(c["q"])
        rows.append({
            "q": c["q"],
            "hit": all(k in out.answer for k in c.get("must_contain", [])),
            "abstained": out.abstained,
            "abstain_correct": (not c["answerable"]) == out.abstained,
        })
    return {
        "dataset": version,
        "run_at": datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        "hit_rate": sum(r["hit"] for r in rows) / len(rows),
        "abstention_accuracy": sum(r["abstain_correct"] for r in rows) / len(rows),
        "rows": rows,
    }

# Store every run:  runs/2026-10-03T05-12.json
# Compare: current run vs previous runs on the SAME dataset version —
# a regression is a delta, not a vibe.
annot: abstain_correct encodes the full 2x2: answerable→answered, unanswerable→abstained — both directions scored
Every run is persisted with its dataset version — comparison across time is apples-to-apples
must_contain keeps the check structural (facts present), robust to phrasing variation

notes:
# Eval Fundamentals

## Why evals
- Change is constant: prompt iterations, silent model updates, living data.
- No eval → quality discovered via complaints.
- Rule: nothing ships without an eval run (same discipline as tests).

## Golden dataset
- 50–200 REAL questions + expert reference answers; quality > size.
- Cover: common · edge · adversarial · **unanswerable** (abstention).
- Versioned (golden-v1, v2…); never leak into prompts/training.
- Owner + quarterly review; stale gold is worse than none.

## Offline vs online
- **Offline**: golden set, reproducible, gates releases.
- **Online**: shadow judging, user feedback, canary analysis; monitors drift.
- Alert on DELTAS, not single scores.

## Human review loops
- Rubric + calibration (shared cases, Cohen's kappa).
- Sample: random + flagged (low scores, thumbs-down, abstentions).
- Humans calibrate machines; review volume shrinks as judges improve.
